title: Forces and momentum
intro: Forces explain **why** things move the way they do. In this lesson you'll build up from what a force is to one of the most useful ideas in physics: conservation of momentum.
objectives: Represent forces as vectors and draw free-body diagrams
Use Newton's three laws of motion
Calculate momentum $p = mv$ and impulse $J = F\Delta t$
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and explosions

steps.title: Forces are vectors
steps.body:
A force is a push or a pull. It has a size (measured in newtons, N) **and** a direction, so it is a vector.

To work out what an object will do, we draw a **free-body diagram**: the object on its own, with an arrow for every force acting *on* it. Each arrow starts on the object and its length shows the size of the force.

figure.caption: A box pulled along a table. Four forces act on it.

steps.key: Only draw forces acting **on** the object, never forces the object exerts on other things.

check.question: In the diagram, which pair of forces cancels if the box does not lift off or sink into the table?
check.explain: Vertically nothing accelerates, so the normal force balances the weight.

steps.title: Newton's first law
steps.body:
An object stays at rest, or keeps moving at **constant velocity**, unless a resultant (unbalanced) force acts on it.

This means a force is not needed to *keep* something moving; a force is needed to *change* its motion. The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion is called **inertia**.
steps.key: Resultant force = 0  ⇔  constant velocity (which includes being at rest).

check.question: A space probe far from any planet switches off its engines. What happens to its motion?
options: It keeps moving at constant velocity
It starts to move in a circle
check.explain: With no resultant force there is no acceleration, so its velocity stays the same.

steps.title: Newton's second law
steps.body: When a resultant force acts, the object accelerates in the direction of the force. For a constant mass:
steps.example:
A $1500\text{ kg}$ car accelerates at $2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The resultant force is $F = 1500 \times 2.0 = 3000\text{ N}$.

The more general form is $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$: force is the rate of change of momentum. You'll use this in step 5.

check.question: The same resultant force acts on two trolleys. Trolley Y has twice the mass of trolley X. How does the acceleration of Y compare with X?
check.explain: $a = F/m$, so doubling the mass halves the acceleration.

steps.title: Newton's third law
steps.body:
When body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts a force on body A that is **equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type**.

The two forces in a pair always act on **different** bodies, so they never cancel each other out.

check.question: A book rests on a table. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with the Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
options: The table's normal force on the book
The book's gravitational pull on the Earth
The book's push on the table
check.explain: The pair must be the same type of force (gravity) acting on the other body (the Earth). The normal force is a different type of force, so it is not the pair even though it balances the weight.

steps.title: Momentum and impulse
steps.body: **Momentum** is mass × velocity. It is a vector, measured in $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ (or N s).

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 240" width="420" role="img" aria-label="Force-time graph: area equals impulse"><defs><marker id="ah13233A" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" fill="#13233A"/></marker></defs><path d="M60 190 C 120 190, 140 60, 200 60 C 260 60, 280 190, 340 190 Z" fill="#0E9F8E" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#0E9F8E" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="390" y2="200" stroke="#13233A" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah13233A)"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="25" stroke="#13233A" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah13233A)"/><text x="385" y="225" fill="#13233A" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="end">time t</text><text x="50" y="30" fill="#13233A" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="end">F</text><text x="200" y="140" fill="#13233A" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">Area = impulse = Δp</text></svg>
figure.caption: When the force changes, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph.

steps.key: Increasing the time of an impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum. That is how airbags, crumple zones and bending your knees on landing protect you.

check.question: A $0.50\text{ kg}$ ball hits a wall at $4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and bounces straight back at $4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the size of its change in momentum?
check.explain: Velocity changes from $+4.0$ to $-4.0$, so $\Delta p = 0.50 \times 8.0 = 4.0\text{ N s}$. Direction matters!

steps.title: Conservation of momentum
steps.body: In an **isolated system** (no external resultant force), the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it. This works for collisions and for explosions.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 230" width="460" role="img" aria-label="Two trolleys before and after sticking together"><defs><marker id="ah0E9F8E" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" fill="#0E9F8E"/></marker><marker id="ahF2994A" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" fill="#F2994A"/></marker></defs><text x="20" y="30" fill="#5B6575" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="start">Before</text><rect x="40" y="45" width="90" height="45" rx="8" fill="#13233A"/><text x="85" y="74" fill="#fff" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">2.0 kg</text><line x1="135" y1="67" x2="205" y2="67" stroke="#F2994A" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#ahF2994A)"/><text x="170" y="58" fill="#F2994A" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">3.0 m/s</text><rect x="250" y="45" width="60" height="45" rx="8" fill="#5B6575"/><text x="280" y="74" fill="#fff" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">1.0 kg</text><text x="380" y="74" fill="#5B6575" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">at rest</text><line x1="20" y1="120" x2="440" y2="120" stroke="#E6E2D8" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><text x="20" y="150" fill="#5B6575" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="start">After</text><rect x="150" y="165" width="90" height="45" rx="8" fill="#13233A"/><rect x="240" y="165" width="60" height="45" rx="8" fill="#5B6575"/><text x="225" y="194" fill="#fff" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle">3.0 kg</text><line x1="305" y1="187" x2="375" y2="187" stroke="#0E9F8E" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#ah0E9F8E)"/><text x="340" y="178" fill="#0E9F8E" font-family="Inter, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">v = ?</text></svg>
figure.caption: A 2.0 kg trolley collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together.

steps.example:
Total momentum before $= 2.0 \times 3.0 + 1.0 \times 0 = 6.0\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.

After: $3.0\,v = 6.0$, so $v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Kinetic energy before $= 9.0\text{ J}$, after $= 6.0\text{ J}$. Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not: this collision is **inelastic**.

check.question: A $60\text{ kg}$ skater at rest throws a $3.0\text{ kg}$ ball forwards at $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the skater's recoil speed?
check.explain: Total momentum stays zero: $60\,v = 3.0 \times 10$, so $v = 0.50\text{ m s}^{-1}$ backwards.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Draw free-body diagrams with only the forces acting **on** the object.
- Resultant force zero means constant velocity (first law).
- $F = ma$, or more generally $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ (second law).
- Force pairs are equal, opposite, same type and act on different bodies (third law).
- Impulse $F\Delta t = \Delta p$ = area under an F–t graph.
- In an isolated system, momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.

Now test yourself on real questions.
